metadata.title: Claude, Exam Forecast.
metadata.subtitle: What an Exam-Forecast Skill Actually Promises
metadata.purpose: Take apart what an exam-forecast skill actually is: a counting mechanism run against public course material, output as a ranked list. Lands the carry-out that it doesn't show you the exam — it reorders your study time.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B07 (a ranked three-slot list: planted blank, then filled in)
metadata.one_flag: B06 (the forecast only works where a pattern already exists)

beats.narration_text: Newcomer assumption: Claude reads the textbook, tells you exactly what's on the exam. It can't — it ranks topics by likelihood. Different machine entirely. So what does exam-forecast really promise? Liam, in for Bear.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Claude reads my textbook and tells me EXACTLY what's on the exam.', hesitates on 'exactly', corrects to 'roughly', lands the real question

props.text:

What does it really promise?

beats.narration_text: Here's what's actually happening at finals: fourteen weeks of reading compressed into days. Read it sequentially from page one and the clock runs out before the content does. Something has to give — either you skip material, or you reorder it. Reorder is the interesting choice.

production_viz.label: NOT ENOUGH TIME TO REREAD
production_viz.caption: time runs out before content does

beats.narration_text: Concrete case. Contracts final, three weeks out. Feed the skill two files — your syllabus and every past exam you can find — and it hands back a ranked list. Three slots. Topic one, two, three. Empty for now; the mechanism goes here.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — three blank ranked slots

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — A RANKED LIST
production_viz.caption: what your Contracts final forecast will look like

beats.narration_text: The intuitive read on the word 'forecast': Claude somehow saw this year's exam and is handing you the real questions early. If that were the mechanism, it would be a leak, not a forecast. Different failure mode, different word.

It hasn't and it can't — the professor's exam file sits behind their own login until exam day. The forecast reads something else entirely: the material that's already public. Your syllabus. Old exams. The pattern was there the whole time. The skill just counts it.

shot.new_visual_element: ONE IS LOCKED, ONE IS PUBLIC

production_viz.label: ONE IS LOCKED, ONE IS PUBLIC
production_viz.caption: the forecast comes from what's already public

beats.narration_text: Here's what a Skill actually is: a folder Claude reads before it does the work. Inside is SKILL.md — the recipe. Three steps, in order. Gather the sources you fed in. Count how often each topic showed up on past exams. Rank what's left. Instructions as a plain markdown file, not as code.

production_viz.label: HOW THE SKILL WORKS
production_viz.caption: the file is the instructions, run in order

beats.narration_text: One flag on the whole thing. It only works where a pattern already exists. A brand-new course leaves nothing to count. A professor who rewrites the format every year has erased the pattern on purpose. They optimized the exam for teaching, not for prediction — and prediction is exactly what the forecast needs. No history, no forecast.

Back to the Contracts final. Same three slots, now filled. Consideration doctrine first — it's been on the exam four of the last five years. Statute of frauds second. Then the narrower exceptions. The output is a ranked list because the input was a count. The shape of the answer tracks the shape of the question.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — same three slots, filled in

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — THE RANKED LIST
production_viz.caption: ranked by pattern, not memorized answers

beats.narration_text: Ranked first doesn't mean guaranteed. Consideration doctrine could still sit out this particular year — a pattern is exactly the kind of thing that can break once. The forecast is a probability, judged from the past. Not a certainty about the future.

And ranked low doesn't mean safe to skip. The bottom of the list is still on the list — a low-ranked topic can be exactly the curveball the professor uses to see who actually read. The forecast reorders your study time. It never deletes a topic from the exam.

shot.new_visual_element: RANKED LOW ISN'T SAFE TO SKIP

production_viz.label: RANKED LOW ISN'T SAFE TO SKIP
chips: STILL COULD BE ON THE PAGE
production_viz.caption: the list re-orders study time, it never deletes a topic

beats.narration_text: Exam forecast doesn't show you the exam. It shows you where the class has been leaning — a rank order for your study time, not a shortcut past it.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I have a final in three weeks. Here's my syllabus and reading list — read them. Then, if I share past exams for the course, count how often each topic has appeared. Rank what's left by how often it's actually been tested, and tell me where to start studying first. Go deeper: take the top-ranked topic and give me a one-week study plan that reflects exactly how it's been tested before.
